data.title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents
data.description:
Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.

Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.

The decision to limit the Mac feature also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.

AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.

In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.

“Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems… without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers.

The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.”

“Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.

Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.

data.title: Circuit Breaker Labs hopes to make AI safer for your kids (and you)
data.description:
With all the talk about how AI might one day kill us all, it’s easy to forget that AI has already been life-threatening to some, not through bioweapons, but psychologically.

For example, Character.AI settled several wrongful death lawsuits earlier this year brought by families of underage users who died by suicide after interactions with its bots. Multiple families have also sued OpenAI over ChatGPT’s alleged role in their loved ones’ suicides and delusions.

Making AI safer across languages and cultures is the mission of Circuit Breaker Labs, one of TechCrunch’s 2026 Startup Battlefield 200 finalists. (Circuit Breaker will be pitching at TechCrunch Disrupt, which takes place at Moscone West in San Francisco from October 13-15, 2026.)

Founders Shirali and Arul Nigam, who are siblings, were motivated by Sewell Setzer, the 14-year-old who developed an emotional attachment to a Character.ai chatbot and confessed thoughts to it of harming himself before dying by suicide. The chatbot, the parents alleged in a 2024 lawsuit, encouraged him. The bot may not have understood what words like “I want to be with you” really implied, said Arul Nigam, who is Circuit Breaker Labs’ CTO.

“A lot of people, especially young people, turn to these systems for support, and usually they aren’t actually getting the help they need. But in many cases, they’re actively being harmed, and people unfortunately have taken their lives already,” Nigam said. “Those sorts of safety vulnerabilities, where people aren’t necessarily actively trying to break the system — they’re engaging in a natural way — and the system has context pollution or it doesn’t understand the nuance, and then takes really dangerous action, we’re trying to prevent that.”

Circuit Breaker Labs has created AI agents that it likens to an army of crash-test dummies. These agents mimic folks from all ages, backgrounds, languages, cultures, and are used to test models on their ability to detect dangerous, psychologically harmful interactions.

“The way a six-year-old girl versus a 45-year-old man, or someone who speaks English as a first language versus a second language, or … gamer slang versus someone else who uses a different kind of slang, all of those can really trip up a model,” said Shirali Nigam, who is Circuit Breaker Labs’ CEO. “Models are really good at handling standard speech patterns, but nobody actually talks like that and so if the model misunderstands nuance or slang, it can go really badly.”

The startup works with human domain experts to build its hyper-realistic user simulations in order to run “red-team” tests against models, which are adversarial tests meant to uncover weaknesses. The tests are built to reflect real human speech patterns, slang, coded language and typos. Circuit Breaker Labs then runs tens of thousand to hundreds of thousands of simulated interactions per day.

The idea is to ensure that a model can appropriately respond to risky interactions that may emerge over time, and many conversations. Circuit Breaker Labs then uses a proprietary scoring method that to create auditable, explainable scores.

Circuit Breaker Labs is currently operating as an AI safety testing lab for high-risk AI applications such as AI coaching, journaling, or other mental health support apps, though Arul Nigam declined to name its marquee customers. Although the startup has a working product, it is in the very early stages, with only five employees including the Nigam siblings.

Eventually, though, the testing platform could be applied to any app where someone may fall down an “AI psychosis” hole, where the human is at risk of developing a parasocial relationship with a chatbot. Examples include AI “co-worker” agents, whose reponses can vary from one interaction to the next.

“People are becoming more skeptical of AI or more resistant to adopt it across the board,” Arul Nigam said, adding that while skepticism is healthy, banning a potentially valuable tool over safety concerns would be “regressive.”

Circuit Breakers Labs believes the answer to those fears is making AI safer. “We want to help build that trust for people.”

Come learn much more about Circuit Breaker Labs and many other innovative startups that have been vetted by TechCrunch at our Startup Battlefield competition, happening in downtown San Francisco on October 13-15.

data.title: Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery to become Skydance
data.description:
Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will operate as Skydance once their merger closes, Paramount CEO David Ellison announced Friday. Skydance is the name of Ellison’s original film production company.

The roughly $110 billion deal is expected to close October 6. It will combine two major Hollywood studios, Paramount+ and HBO Max, and networks including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network. Skydance will also control franchises such as “The Lord of the Rings,” “Game of Thrones,” the DC Universe, and “Yellowstone.”

The merger followed a drawn-out corporate battle. Netflix had agreed to acquire Warner Bros.’ streaming and studio businesses before the broader Paramount deal moved forward. Twelve states challenged the deal, arguing it could reduce competition and harm consumers and workers, but a judge approved a settlement with the state attorneys general this week.

Ellison said the Paramount and Warner Bros. brands will remain central. “We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one,” he wrote on X. The new name, he said, gives the company “an identity of its own” while letting both studios “remain in the spotlight.”

data.title: Pope Leo XIV is not a fan of AI-generated art
data.description:
Critics of AI-generated art have a powerful new ally: His Holiness the Bishop of Rome (Episcopus Romanus), Primate of Italy (Primatus Italiae), and Supreme Pontiff of the Universal Church (Summus Pontifex Ecclesiae Universalis).

In a post on X Friday morning, Pope Leo XIV detailed the spiritual difference between human-generated art and art that is generated by machines, as part of a call to preserve human art from the encroachment of AI.

“In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce,” the Servus Servorum Dei wrote. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.”

Pope Leo XIV gave a more detailed statement on AI in an encyclical letter in May, which emphasized the importance of human dignity in a world of increasing automation.

But that hasn’t stopped AI companies from lobbying the supreme pontiff. According to a recent New York Times report, Anthropic has actively lobbied the Vatican to reconsider its position on non-human consciousness — apparently finding little success.

data.title: Laytr’s new app lets you save anything you find online, not just articles to read
data.description:
After Mozilla’s read-it-later app Pocket shut down in August, a number of alternatives popped up to take its place. But one newcomer, Laytr, is taking things further than offering a way to save things to read. The app lets you save anything on the web for later consumption, whether that’s an article, recipe, screenshot, video, PDF, bookmark, or tab.

The app also automatically sorts those different file types and lets you organize them into collections it calls “cases.” It can also remind you about a saved item on a date you choose, which could help you remember local events or places you want to visit on certain days, for instance. (Or perhaps as a way to force you to get through your reading list!)

What’s interesting about how the app works is that everything you save becomes a private archive that’s only accessible on your own device. That means you don’t have to create an account to use Laytr, and the developer can’t see anything you’ve saved either. Still, you can access your content across multiple Apple devices, including iPhone, iPad, and Mac, because the content syncs over iCloud.

The idea for Laytr comes from Ontario-area indie developer Mostafa Talaat, and is published under his company’s name, Waitery Inc. Talaat told TechCrunch he was inspired to build his own read-it-later app after hearing about Pocket’s shutdown. Creating an app without a server was a privacy choice on his part.

“What you save says a lot about you, and I didn’t want to be holding it. Everything stays on your device and in your own iCloud,” Talaat explained. “When you save something, Laytr asks when you want it back and reminds you on that day. It also imports your old Pocket export, so nobody has to start over,” he added.

Because the app is privacy-focused, there are things it won’t do, including personalizing a feed or using AI to summarize or automatically tag items.

The app is free to try, but limits you to 30 saved items. For full access, the app’s Premium tier costs either $1.99 a month, $14.99 a year, or a one-time $39.99 for a lifetime plan. (The lifetime offering is on sale for $24.99 until the end of December.) Talaat said the the app will focus on adding more languages over time.

If your subscription lapses, you also won’t lose your saves — you just won’t be able to add more until you rejoin a plan or get your archive back under the 30-item limit for free plans. You can also leave Laytr at any time, as the entire archive can be exported as a ZIP file, with readable Markdown and HTML for every item, note, tag, date, and collection (aka “case”).

data.title: Slovenia’s .si domain sees a surge in registrations after Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ order
data.description:
In not-so-surprising news, the .si domain name is seeing unprecedented demand after President Trump signed an executive order mandating all government agencies to refer to “AI” and “artificial intelligence” as “SI” and “super intelligence.” It echoes what happened at the start of the AI boom, when interest in the .ai domain name—associated with the country Anguilla—spiked and brought in millions for the island territory. 

Now it’s .si’s turn in the spotlight. The domain name was commonly associated with Slovenia, where, ironically, First Lady Melania Trump is from. Klara Herman, a spokesperson at Registry SI, the official organization that manages Slovenia’s domains, told the BBC earlier this week that there was a 2,199% increase in .si domain name purchases in September. However, she was cautious about linking the boost only to President Trump.

Still, the Registry noted 11,000 new addresses recorded on September 30th, the day after President Trump signed the executive order, and almost 13,000 new .si domain names were registered in the past 24 hours. 

We reached out to a few other web hosting sites to see if they had seen similar trends. GoDaddy said they don’t yet host the .si domain, and Squarespace hadn’t yet responded as of the time of publication. Wix, interestingly enough, said that they weren’t seeing any “meaningful uptick” on their end, and that it’s been minimal on the site since September 29th. “It’s still early so that could change,” a Wix spokesperson said. 

But web hosting platform Hostinger told me that .si is now its second most popular domain extension, right after .com. It found that among its customers, almost 4,300 registered .si on September 30th and about 5,400 on October 1st; more than three-quarters of all .si domains registered since September 23 came in the last two days. It found that more than half the buyers were coming from the U.S. and India. 

Curiously enough, on Hostinger, only around 3% of the .si domains are explicitly related to AI, it said. Most are “unclassified,” — meaning their names don’t match any specific category. It said that most of those registering the .si domain name seem to be people and businesses, though there is a speculative element, in that people could be buying the domains to resell them later. 

Upon hearing this, my first thought went back to what a founder messaged me earlier this week, noting that .si domains were reselling for over a million dollars. Kim Than, CEO of Genius PR, who specializes in working with AI and crypto founders, told me that he already bought the .si version of his company name “to protect the brand in case this takes off like .ai.” And did so because it was cheap, so he figured he might as well “secure it now than potentially pay a lot more later.”

Than sees domain names as digital collectibles and wants to pick up a few more while the price is still good, and he might resell them later; one can also tokenize domains, he said, and trade them on the blockchain, though he’s not sure if .si is supported just yet. “A few founder friends are buying too cause we think it’s the new AI boom,” he continued. “Who knows how far it goes, but I’m happy to take a bet.”  

There is a chance that .si could become pretty popular. President Trump’s executive order said that “the capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence,” and that they “increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence but a new super intelligence.” 

Klaudijus Januitis, head of domains at Hostinger, told me that he expects the demand for .si to keep growing, though he doesn’t see that domain as replacing .ai anytime soon. Instead, as noted by that founder and his friends, Januitis said .si is right now a more available and a “more affordable second option.” 

“Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw,” he said, noting that, for one, Anguilla charges a “premium” to use .si and that money goes straight to the government, while .si is a fraction of the cost and goes to the registry rather than the treasury. For example, on Hostinger, .si costs around $12 dollars a year while .ai goes for $90 and requires a two-year commitment. “For Anguilla, .ai became a second economy. For Slovenia, .si is a nice bonus.”

data.title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Clay’s Kareem Amin on the rise of the GTM engineer
data.description:
Two years ago, most companies didn’t have a GTM engineer. Now the role is showing up across tech, with practitioners using AI and automation to build revenue systems that once required multiple people, tools, and manual processes.

What changed — and what does it mean for the way companies find customers and grow?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Clay co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin will take the AI Stage for “The GTM Engineer: How AI Created Tech’s Next Big Job Category.” He’ll trace how AI has changed the traditional go-to-market stack and helped create a new discipline in its place, giving attendees a look at what AI-native GTM looks like in practice and how it’s changing company growth.

AI is giving go-to-market teams new ways to research prospects, work with data, personalize outreach, and automate workflows that once moved between separate tools and teams. As those capabilities converge, companies are rethinking not only their GTM technology, but who builds and manages the systems behind growth.

If you’re building a company or rethinking how your team approaches sales, marketing, and growth, this is a new role worth understanding. Secure your Disrupt pass and see where GTM engineering fits into the next generation of go-to-market. Get a second pass at a 50% discount, and more savings for groups of four or more.

What does a GTM engineer actually do?

Traditional go-to-market work can involve hours of researching accounts, cleaning data, qualifying leads, preparing outreach, and moving information between systems. GTM engineering uses AI, data, and automation to turn more of that work into repeatable systems.

Clay coined the role in 2023. Its own GTM engineering guide describes GTM engineers as practitioners who build automated revenue workflows rather than executing individual GTM tasks by hand. The company says roughly 100 GTM engineering job listings are now appearing each month, including roles at companies such as Cursor, Lovable, and Webflow.

For founders and GTM leaders deciding where to put their next dollar or whether to make their next hire, this session offers another way to think about growth. Do you add more people to execute the existing process, or build systems that let the people you already have execute differently?

At Disrupt, Amin will put the shift into context and explore what AI-native GTM looks like in practice. Get your ticket to Disrupt to understand a role that barely existed a few years ago but could change how your next sales, marketing, or growth team operates.

Clay puts AI to work across the GTM stack

Clay started in Brooklyn in 2017 with a goal: give more people access to the power of programming. Its original spreadsheet let users connect information and automate work without writing code. When salespeople, growth teams, and agencies began using it to find and reach customers, Clay followed them into go-to-market.

Today, the company provides infrastructure for GTM teams to access data, run agentic workflows and launch campaigns. Its OpenAI-powered agent, Claygent, automates research and outreach for sales, marketing and recruiting teams.

That evolution has been accompanied by rapid growth. TechCrunch reported in February that the company had tripled annual recurring revenue to $100 million in a year and announced an employee tender offer at a $5 billion valuation. Clay has continued growing since then, announcing a $115 million Series D in September at a $7.1 billion valuation.

Clay is also investing directly in the job category at the center of Amin’s Disrupt session, announcing a $1 million scholarship fund in September to train GTM engineers.

For companies trying to determine where AI can make a meaningful difference in revenue operations, add Amin’s session to your Disrupt agenda and see how one company is putting that model into practice.

From product leader to a new GTM approach

Kareem Amin co-founded Clay in 2017 and serves as its co-founder and CEO. Before Clay, he was VP of product at The Wall Street Journal and co-founded collaboration startup Frame, which Sailthru acquired in 2012.

Amin started Clay around the idea of putting programming capabilities into more people’s hands. AI eventually gave that idea a new application: enabling GTM teams to build systems that automate research, data enrichment, and outreach without relying on traditional engineering resources for every workflow.

Want to understand what a GTM engineer could mean for your own growth strategy? Secure your Disrupt pass and hear directly from one of the founders helping define the category.

See what AI-native GTM looks like in practice at Disrupt

“The GTM Engineer: How AI Created Tech’s Next Big Job Category” is one of 200+ sessions across six industry stages, roundtables, and breakouts at Disrupt, October 13–15 at Moscone West in San Francisco. More than 10,000 founders, investors, operators, and tech leaders are expected, along with 250+ speakers and 300+ exhibiting startups.

Beyond the sessions, matchmaking, dealmaking, and networking give attendees opportunities to meet potential customers, investors, partners, and other founders confronting many of the same growth challenges.

GTM engineering may be a new job category, but the problem it addresses isn’t: how do you find and reach the right customers without simply adding more people and more tools? At Disrupt, you can see how AI is changing that equation — and meet the people building what comes next.
